document_title: 「海草復育」溫室氣體減量方法 — Marine Blue-Carbon Voluntary Reduction Method
notes: Taiwan's Ministry of Environment formally approved and published the Seagrass Restoration greenhouse-gas reduction method in 2025 under the voluntary reduction mechanism. The method treats active seagrass planting and supporting hydrological, sediment, salinity and water-quality management as a project intervention that increases organic-carbon storage in marine/coastal or artificial wetlands. It restricts biological removal within the project boundary except where necessary for seagrass protection and requires environmental-impact analysis and public consultation. The wider voluntary-reduction framework requires measurable, reportable and verifiable outcomes, additionality, conservativeness and permanence, with project-specific third-party validation before registration. The method creates an accounting and crediting route for additional seagrass carbon-sink projects; it does not mean that ordinary seagrass conservation without an eligible project intervention automatically generates credits.
source: Taiwan Ministry of Environment — Climate Change Administration / Voluntary Reduction and Offset Information Platform
status_note: Approved on 24 July 2025 and formally published for use on the Ministry of Environment voluntary-reduction platform in September 2025.

document_title: 「紅樹林植林」溫室氣體減量方法 — Marine Blue-Carbon Voluntary Reduction Method
notes: Taiwan's Ministry of Environment formally approved and published the Mangrove Afforestation greenhouse-gas reduction method in 2025 under the voluntary reduction mechanism. It applies to planting mangroves within eligible human-made wetlands such as idle salt pans, aquaculture ponds and other ponds, subject to project-boundary and prior-land-use conditions intended to avoid displacement and leakage. Projects must select locally appropriate mangrove species, manage hydrology, sediment, salinity and water quality, prevent planted mangroves from spreading beyond the boundary, and conduct environmental-impact analysis and public consultation. The method provides a formal route for quantifying additional organic-carbon storage and applying for voluntary reduction units; it is not a blanket credit for existing mangrove stocks or ordinary protection without an eligible project activity.
source: Taiwan Ministry of Environment — Climate Change Administration / Voluntary Reduction and Offset Information Platform
status_note: Approved on 24 July 2025 and formally published for use on the Ministry of Environment voluntary-reduction platform in September 2025.

document_title: Offshore Wind-Farm Artificial Surface Seaweed Farm Carbon-Sink Demonstration
notes: Taiwan's Fisheries Research Institute and the National Academy of Marine Research reported the first successful cultivation of large macroalgae in domestic offshore-wind-farm waters in 2023. Under the Ministry of Agriculture's Natural Carbon Sink Key Strategic Action Plan, the programme first established land-based algal mass-production capacity in Qigu, then deployed an improved artificial surface seaweed-farm facility near an offshore-wind meteorological tower and tested multiple macroalgal species. The trial measured survival and biomass growth and was explicitly framed as technology development for marine algal carbon sinks and shared use of wind-farm and fishery space. The official source estimated scaling potential, but those estimates are prospective; the record therefore represents an R&D/demonstration practice rather than independently verified durable net CO2 removal or an issued carbon credit.
source: Taiwan Ministry of Agriculture — Fisheries Research Institute / National Academy of Marine Research
status_note: The specific 2023 offshore cultivation trial was completed and publicly reported on 23 October 2023; related marine-carbon-sink R&D continued under the Natural Carbon Sink strategy.

subnational_area: Incheon Metropolitan City; Yeongheung thermal-power-site application context
document_title: Incheon IMTA CO2-Reduction R&D Project (2023–2025)
notes: Incheon Metropolitan City's Fisheries Resources Research Institute and Incheon National University launched a 30-month, KRW 420 million field-technology R&D project selected through Korea South-East Power to study CO2 reduction using Integrated Multi-Trophic Aquaculture (IMTA). The system was designed to reuse wastes and nutrients from fed aquaculture through organisms including shellfish and seaweed, while the official project description specifically identifies CO2 capture by seaweed as a targeted benefit. A land-based IMTA system was constructed to assess production, organic and inorganic nutrient removal and seaweed CO2 absorption, including a prospective waste-heat/cooling-water application at the Yeongheung power complex. The project is retained as an explicit IMTA carbon-sink research practice; shellfish are not independently tagged as a carbon-sink pathway because the source attributes the direct CO2-capture function to seaweed rather than demonstrating net shellfish removal.
source: Incheon Metropolitan City — Fisheries Resources Research Institute / Incheon National University / Korea South-East Power
status_note: Launched in 2023 for 30 months; Incheon's later programme reporting lists the IMTA research as a completed 2024–2025 activity and a basis for new carbon-sink research.

document_title: Korea–U.S. Joint Seaweed Biomass Production System Technology Development Programme
notes: In 2025 Incheon Fisheries Resources Research Institute was selected to participate in the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries' Korea–U.S. joint Seaweed Biomass Production System Technology Development programme. The five-year, KRW 41 billion programme shares Korean and U.S. technology and data to develop offshore mass-cultivation systems, seaweed-based carbon-reduction technologies and an AI-enabled integrated aquaculture-management platform, with digitalization and standardization aimed at later industrialization. It is therefore a government-funded macroalgal carbon-sink R&D programme, not proof that harvested biomass already constitutes durable verified carbon removal or that credits have been issued.

document_title: Environment Protection (Sea Dumping) Amendment (Using New Technologies to Fight Climate Change) Act 2023 — Marine Geoengineering Research Permitting
notes: Australia's 2023 Sea Dumping amendment became an Act and amended the national sea-dumping framework to enable permits for the placement of wastes or other matter for a marine geoengineering activity for the purpose of scientific research, implementing obligations associated with the 2013 London Protocol marine-geoengineering amendment. For the strict ONCE database, the record is tagged to ocean fertilization because that is the marine-geoengineering activity currently listed under the London Protocol regulatory architecture; the Act is not treated as blanket authorization for OAE, biomass sinking or other emerging mCDR techniques. Its separate provisions concerning export and subseabed storage of captured CO2 are not coded here as marine geological CDR storage because those provisions can also serve conventional point-source CCS and do not by themselves establish a negative-emissions chain. Any research proposal remains subject to permit assessment and environmental safeguards.
source: Parliament of Australia / Australian Government
status_note: Act received Royal Assent in November 2023; project-specific marine-geoengineering research remains subject to the Sea Dumping Act permit and assessment framework.

document_title: Catching Marine Carbon: Testing Ocean Solutions for Climate Mitigation using Natural Analogues — MBIE Endeavour Programme END25304
notes: This five-year MBIE Endeavour programme (2025–2030) explicitly evaluates three proposed marine carbon dioxide removal approaches through natural analogues in New Zealand waters: alkalinity addition, deep-ocean deposition of terrestrial biomass, and nutrient addition to enhance phytoplankton carbon uptake and deep export. The programme develops measurement and verification protocols, environmental-risk assessment guidance, a national marine carbon budget and policy/governance uptake pathways. Field campaigns use natural river/submarine-groundwater alkalinity inputs, cyclone-deposited seafloor wood and natural phytoplankton blooms as analogues rather than authorizing deliberate full-scale deployment. The record is therefore a government-funded mCDR research and MRV practice, not evidence that these interventions are already permitted, creditable or effective at scale.
source: Earth Sciences New Zealand (NIWA) / New Zealand Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment — Endeavour Fund
status_note: Five-year Endeavour Fund programme running from 2025 to 2030; project END25304 field activities were underway in 2026.

notes: The UK government's GBP 60 million Direct Air Capture and Greenhouse Gas Removal Innovation Programme, part of the Net Zero Innovation Portfolio, explicitly funded first-of-a-kind demonstration and pilot plants including seawater solutions and direct ocean capture. document_title: Marine and Fisheries 2050 Carbon Neutrality Roadmap — From Carbon Neutrality to Carbon Negative
notes: The Republic of Korea's Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries announced the Marine and Fisheries 2050 Carbon Neutrality Roadmap in December 2021. The roadmap sets a sectoral 2050 net greenhouse-gas target and uses blue-carbon expansion as a major sink pillar. It calls for restoration of damaged tidal flats, large-scale tidal-flat vegetation restoration and sea-forest creation. It also says research will be expanded to identify additional blue-carbon sources such as seaweed, shellfish and microalgae. Under the strict ONCE boundary, the explicit anthropogenic coastal-restoration actions are coded as engineering pathways, while the mere listing of microalgae, seaweed and shellfish as candidate additional blue carbon is retained as research context and is not by itself treated as a microalgae-fixation or aquaculture sink-engineering pathway.
source: Republic of Korea Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries
status_note: National marine-and-fisheries carbon-neutrality roadmap announced on 16 December 2021.

notes: Ocean Visions released this dedicated microalgae carbon dioxide removal road map on 22 February 2023. Priorities include controlled field trials, siting, scalable cultivation/sequestration systems, responsible-research codes and governance frameworks. The road map explicitly concerns long-duration carbon removal rather than ordinary algal production or short-lived biomass utilization, so it is retained as pathway-specific ONCE research and governance.
source: Ocean Visions

document_title: Harnessing Carbon Removal Opportunities in Wastewater Treatment
notes: RMI's May 2026 brief assesses how carbon dioxide removal can be integrated into municipal and biogenic-industrial wastewater treatment. It explicitly distinguishes Wastewater Alkalinity Enhancement (WAE), which reacts alkaline feedstocks with biogenic CO2 within treatment processes, from OAE using alkalinity-rich outflows to drive subsequent atmospheric CO2 uptake in rivers or oceans. The brief discusses baseline and additionality challenges, feedstock life-cycle emissions, emerging accounting protocols, infrastructure integration, scale-up constraints and the need for more pilot projects. It is included as a dedicated technology-policy assessment, not as evidence that routine wastewater pH control constitutes CDR.
source: RMI
status_note: Published 29 May 2026 as an active RMI carbon-removal industry brief.

document_title: Removing Carbon Dioxide Through Artificial Upwelling and Downwelling: Legal Challenges and Opportunities
notes: This Sabin Center report is dedicated to the legal governance of artificial upwelling and artificial downwelling as ocean-based CDR. It analyzes how international and U.S. domestic law could apply to systems that deliberately cycle water between the surface and deep ocean to stimulate biological uptake or transfer carbon-rich surface water to depth. The report emphasizes unresolved sequestration efficacy, environmental risks and legal uncertainty. It is included as pathway-specific governance research and does not imply authorization or demonstrated net removal.

document_title: Carbon Capture, Usage and Storage: A Vision to Establish a Competitive Market — GGR Business Model Criteria Covering Seawater CO2 Removal
notes: The UK government's 2023 CCUS market vision describes the Greenhouse Gas Removals (GGR) business-model framework established alongside the Energy Act 2023 and sets criteria for robust negative emissions. The government states that eligible removal must be net-negative, that the CO2 source must be directly from the atmosphere or seawater (through chemical, biological or geochemical means), and that removed carbon must be held in a highly durable store. This creates a national market-policy signal that can encompass direct ocean/seawater carbon removal, distinct from the UK's separate R&D funding for SeaCURE and other pilots. Under the strict ONCE boundary, only the explicit seawater-removal component is coded here; the broader industrial CCUS and fossil point-source storage provisions are not treated as ONCE.
source: UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
status_note: UK government CCUS market vision published in December 2023; the GGR business-model framework and associated policy development remain part of the UK carbon-removal policy architecture.

document_title: Ocean Visions Electrochemical Carbon Dioxide Removal Road Map
notes: Ocean Visions maintains a pathway-specific living road map for electrochemical marine carbon dioxide removal. It defines the approach as anthropogenic CDR that can either remove dissolved inorganic carbon from seawater as CO2 or solid carbonate, or electrochemically produce a reactive base such as NaOH for ocean addition and conversion of atmospheric CO2 into long-lived bicarbonate. The road map notes that these approaches are often grouped under direct ocean capture while also overlapping with electrochemical OAE. It prioritizes controlled field experiments, environmental-impact characterization, autonomous monitoring, new modeling tools and methods to verify additional atmospheric CO2 uptake against the dynamic ocean background. The road map is a research and governance resource, not deployment authorization or evidence that any electrochemical pathway has already achieved durable net removal at scale.
source: Ocean Visions

notes: Ocean Visions released a dedicated road map on 1 December 2023 to advance research on restoring blue-carbon ecosystems as a carbon dioxide removal strategy. The road map covers knowledge gaps, field testing, storage duration, technical restoration challenges and measurement/verification needs across blue-carbon systems. To avoid inflating individual habitat counts, this database codes the record only to the cross-ecosystem coastal-blue-carbon restoration/sink-enhancement pathway rather than automatically tagging every ecosystem named in the overview.

notes: NEDO selected Hokkaido University, with Toho Gas and GS Yuasa, for an FY2026 marine CDR theme developing low-power direct ocean capture using hydrogen-pumping electrodialysis. subnational_area: Japan — seawater-based atmospheric CO2 mineralization research
document_title: ERCA 1CN-2201 — Atmospheric CO2 Fixation as CaCO3 Using Seawater-Inspired Biomineralization
notes: Japan’s Environment Research and Technology Development Fund supported project 1CN-2201 from FY2022 through FY2024 to develop a negative-emissions process that uses seawater as the calcium-ion source and supplied air as the atmospheric CO2 source. The project builds on a polyamine-assisted biomineralization method to synthesize recoverable, low-solubility CaCO3, improve efficiency and cost using fine-bubble air supply, recover and reuse additives, and generate scale-up/process-design data. The official project summary explicitly frames the concept as recovering atmospheric CO2 as CaCO3 and states a negative-emissions objective. Because the carbon source is atmospheric air rather than dissolved inorganic carbon removed from seawater, this record is not coded as DOC; and because it does not rely on open-ocean alkalinity addition to induce air-sea uptake, it is not coded as OAE. It is retained instead as a land-sea-coordinated negative-emissions research practice using seawater resources for durable mineral fixation. The project ended in FY2024 and does not by itself establish commercial deployment or verified lifecycle net removal.
source: Environmental Restoration and Conservation Agency of Japan (ERCA) — Environment Research and Technology Development Fund / University of Tokyo
status_note: Government-funded research project ran from FY2022 through FY2024 and has concluded.

document_title: 2026 Fisheries Resource Management Implementation Plan — 20 Sea-Forest Carbon-Trading Pilot Sites
notes: The Republic of Korea’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries formally announced the 2026 Fisheries Resource Management Implementation Plan under the Fisheries Resources Management Act. The plan operationalizes the broader 2026–2030 fisheries-resource strategy by providing for a sea-forest carbon-trading pilot across 20 sites nationwide, intended to test staged operability across types and sea areas and to contribute to fishing-community income. This record is kept separately from the Fourth Basic Plan because it is the annual implementation instrument that specifies an actual multi-site pilot. To preserve the ONCE boundary, sea-forest restoration and carbon-credit experimentation are coded as coastal blue-carbon restoration/sink enhancement rather than automatically as macroalgae aquaculture: a restored or created seaweed forest is not equivalent to commercial seaweed farming. The plan is a policy implementation measure, not evidence that credits from all pilot sites have already been verified or entered a compliance market.
source: Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, Republic of Korea
status_note: Official 2026 implementation plan announced by the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries on 26 February 2026; 20 sea-forest carbon-trading pilot sites are specified for implementation.
